13176:
Jesus speaks as a Jew — 'we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews' (John 4:22) — while opening the door to Samaritans as part of a restored Israel. The prophets hoped for the reunion of the northern tribes with Judah (Ezek 37:15-22). God himself is 'the fountain of living waters' (Jer 2:13), and the end-time temple would send out life-giving water (Ezek 47:1-12). Jesus offers that water personally.

The Samaritans expected the Taheb, a prophet like Moses (Deut 18:15-18), rather than a Davidic king. Jesus' 'I am he' (egō eimi) is the first of John's 'I am' sayings. Worship 'in Spirit and truth' does not reject place out of contempt; it means the Father seeks worshippers wherever they are, because the true temple is now Jesus himself.
13177: A mixed community of Jews, Samaritans and Gentiles in John's day would hear its own story: the enmity of centuries dissolved around one well. A royal official (probably serving Herod Antipas) trusting Jesus' word without seeing anticipates the Gentile believers 'who have not seen and yet believe' (John 20:29).
13178: Jesus crosses lines of shame, gender and old religious hatred, treats a marginal woman as a theological conversation partner, and makes her a witness. True worship is not owned by any one place or group.
13179: Jacob meets Rachel at a well.
13180: Jacob's land at Shechem, near Sychar.
13181: God the fountain of living waters.
13182: The prophet like Moses, basis of the Samaritan hope.
13183: Origins of the Samaritan population and its mixed worship.
13184: The Samaritan woman was a notorious sinner whose sexual immorality Jesus exposed.
13185: The text never calls her sinful; her marriages may reflect widowhood or divorce. She is a seeker and the first to bring a town to Jesus (Levine, Keener, Lynn Cohick).
13186: Healing on the Sabbath and the Son who works like the Father
13187: At 'a feast of the Jews' Jesus visits the pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem with its five porches, where many sick people lie. He asks a man paralysed for 38 years, 'Do you want to be well?', and tells him to pick up his mat and walk. It is the Sabbath, so the authorities object to the man carrying his mat. When they learn Jesus healed him, they challenge Jesus, who answers: 'My Father is working until now, and I am working.' They seek to kill him because he calls God his own Father, 'making himself equal with God'. Jesus explains that the Son does only what he sees the Father doing, has authority to give life and to judge, and that witnesses testify for him: John the Baptist, his works, the Father, the scriptures and Moses.
13188: For a long time some scholars doubted the pool of Bethesda with five porticoes existed, and treated the detail as symbolic (five books of Moses). Excavations near the Church of St Anne in Jerusalem uncovered a large double pool with a dividing wall, giving four sides plus a middle colonnade: five porches. This is often cited as evidence of the Gospel writer's accurate local knowledge, and the Copper Scroll from Qumran may mention a site called Beth Eshdatayin ('house of the twin pools'). John 5:3b-4 (an angel stirring the water) is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is usually printed in footnotes.
13189: Sabbath was Israel's weekly gift of rest and a sign of the covenant (Exod 31:13-17). Carrying loads from one domain to another was among the activities rabbis classed as work (Jer 17:21-22 already forbids carrying burdens through Jerusalem's gates on the Sabbath), so the objection was a reasonable application of Torah, not pettiness. Jewish teachers also discussed whether God himself rests on the Sabbath; since people are born and die every Sabbath, they agreed God continues to give life and to judge — the very two works Jesus claims (John 5:21-22).
13190:
Jesus does not attack the Sabbath; he enters a Jewish debate about God's own Sabbath work and places himself on God's side of it. In Jewish law an agent (shaliach) acts with the authority of the one who sends him; Jesus speaks as the Son-agent who does exactly what the Father does. Yet 'honour the Son as they honour the Father' (John 5:23) goes beyond an ordinary agent. The 'Son of Man' who receives authority to judge echoes Dan 7:13-14, and the hour when the dead hear his voice echoes Dan 12:2.

The appeal to witnesses follows Deut 19:15: truth is established by two or three witnesses. Moses himself, the great intercessor, will be a witness for Jesus because 'he wrote of me' (John 5:46).
13191: A community accused of breaking with Moses would hear Jesus claim that Moses and the scriptures were on his side. They would also hear that the conflict over the Sabbath was a debate about who Jesus is, not about whether God's law is good.
13192: 'Do you want to be well?' is a disarmingly personal question. Jesus' Sabbath healings show God's rest as restoration. The chapter also warns that it is possible to search the scriptures diligently yet miss the person they point to (John 5:39-40).
13194: Not carrying burdens on the Sabbath.
13195: The Son of Man given authority.
13196: The dead rising to life or judgement.
13197: Two or three witnesses establish a matter.
13198: Jesus broke the Sabbath to show that God's law was legalistic and obsolete.
13199: Jesus engages a Jewish debate about God's life-giving work on the Sabbath and claims to share it; the issue is his identity, not the law's worth (Keener, Levine, Thompson).
13201: Near Passover, by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus feeds five thousand people with five barley loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets of leftovers are gathered. The crowd says he is 'the Prophet who is to come' and wants to make him king by force, so he withdraws. That night the disciples see him walking on the sea; he says 'I am; do not be afraid.' In the synagogue at Capernaum Jesus says he is the bread of life, the true bread from heaven, greater than the manna; whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood has eternal life. Many disciples find this 'a hard saying' and leave. Jesus asks the Twelve if they will go too; Peter answers, 'Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.'
13202: This is the second Passover in John (John 2:13, John 6:4, John 11:55), which is why many say Jesus' ministry lasted about three years. The feeding is the only miracle besides the resurrection found in all four Gospels. The language of eating flesh and drinking blood is widely seen as connected to the Lord's Supper, which John does not narrate at the Last Supper; how directly John means the Eucharist is debated (Catholic and Orthodox readers see a clear reference; many Protestants read it as a vivid image for trusting Jesus' death, see John 6:35 and John 6:47).
13203: Barley loaves were the bread of the poor. The crowd's response follows Passover logic: Passover remembered the exodus, and many Jews hoped the Messiah would come at Passover and that the manna would fall again in the messianic age (2 Baruch 29:8 speaks of manna descending again). A 'prophet like Moses' who fed people in the wilderness was exactly what such hopes looked for. Eating someone's 'flesh' and drinking 'blood' would shock: Torah forbade consuming blood (Lev 17:10-14). Jesus' language is deliberately jarring.
13204:
The chapter is a Passover midrash. The crowd quotes 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat' (Ps 78:24, compare Exod 16:4), and Jesus interprets it like a synagogue teacher: it was not Moses but my Father who gives the true bread from heaven. In Jewish tradition Torah and Wisdom were spoken of as bread: Wisdom invites, 'Come, eat of my bread' (Prov 9:5), and Isaiah calls the thirsty and hungry to come and eat without cost (Isa 55:1-3). Jesus presents himself as God's living Torah-Wisdom-bread.

Walking on the sea with 'I am; do not be afraid' echoes God who 'trampled the waves of the sea' (Job 9:8) and led Israel through the sea at the exodus (Ps 77:19). The grumbling (gongyzō) of the crowd (John 6:41) echoes Israel's murmuring in the wilderness (Exod 16:2). Peter's confession, 'the Holy One of God', is a Jewish title for one set apart by God.
13205: The scene of disciples leaving would resonate with a community that had seen others turn back. Peter's 'to whom shall we go?' spoke for those who stayed despite the cost. Readers who celebrated the Lord's Supper would hear their meal echoed.
13206: Jesus offers himself, not just his gifts. Some follow for loaves; real discipleship is staying when the teaching is hard, because there is nowhere else to find life.
13207: God rains bread from heaven in the wilderness.
13209: Elisha feeds a hundred with barley loaves, with some left over.
13210: Come, eat and drink without cost; hear and live.
13211: God alone treads on the waves of the sea.
13212: Readers either flatten John 6 into a doctrine of the Mass, or dismiss any sacramental meaning as pure metaphor.
13213: The chapter is first a Passover-manna midrash about trusting Jesus as God's bread; whether and how it points to the Eucharist is a genuine debate between traditions (Brown, Carson, Keener).
13215: At the feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot) Jesus' brothers, who do not believe in him, urge him to show himself in Judea. He goes up quietly, then teaches openly in the temple halfway through the feast. People argue: is he a good man or a deceiver? Has he studied? Is he the Messiah? Can the Messiah come from Galilee? On the last great day of the feast Jesus stands and cries out, 'If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the scripture said, out of his heart will flow rivers of living water' — which John explains as the Spirit. The temple guards fail to arrest him ('No one ever spoke like this man'), and Nicodemus urges a fair hearing.
13216: Chapters 7 to 10:21 are set at Sukkot, the autumn feast. The debate over Jesus' origin (Galilee, Bethlehem, unknown) reflects real Jewish discussions about how the Messiah would appear (John 7:27, John 7:42). Fear 'of the Jews' among people who are themselves Jews (John 7:13) shows that 'the Jews' here means the Jerusalem authorities. The fact that even Jesus' brothers did not believe (John 7:5) is a striking admission that early Christians would hardly invent; James later became a leader in Jerusalem (Gal 1:19).
13217: Sukkot was the most joyful pilgrimage feast. Families lived in booths for seven days, remembering the wilderness (Lev 23:42-43), and gave thanks for the harvest. According to the Mishnah (Sukkah 4-5), each morning a priest drew water from the pool of Siloam in a golden pitcher and processed to the temple, where it was poured on the altar with wine while the Hallel Psalms (Ps 113-118) were sung. It was also a prayer for the coming winter rains. The rabbis said whoever had not seen the rejoicing of the water-drawing had never seen joy. On the seventh day, the priests circled the altar seven times. Into that scene Jesus cries, 'Come to me and drink.'
13218:
The water ritual looked back to water from the rock in the wilderness (Exod 17:6, Ps 78:15-16) and forward to the end-time river flowing from the temple (Ezek 47:1-12) and the living waters going out from Jerusalem on the day when all nations would keep Sukkot (Zech 14:8, Zech 14:16). Isaiah tied it together: 'With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation' (Isa 12:3), and God promised to pour water on the thirsty and his Spirit on Israel's offspring (Isa 44:3).

Jesus claims that the hope of the feast is fulfilled in him: from him (or from the believer, the Greek can be read either way) flow rivers of the Spirit. He is standing at the heart of Israel's worship, using its own words, at its own feast. The debate about him is a Jewish debate among Jews about the Messiah.
13219: Readers far from Jerusalem, possibly cut off from festival life, would hear that the joy and the Spirit promised at Sukkot had not been taken from them: they flowed from Jesus. The divided crowd also mirrored their own experience of families split over Jesus.
13220: The Spirit is not an abstract doctrine but the satisfaction of a deep thirst. The chapter also shows honest uncertainty about Jesus, and Nicodemus models a quiet courage: insisting on fairness when a group rushes to judgement.
13221: The feast of booths and its rejoicing.
13223: The river from the temple bringing life.
13224: Drawing water from the wells of salvation.
13225: Water on thirsty ground and the Spirit poured out.
13226: The light of the world and 'before Abraham was, I am'
13227: Most modern Bibles first print the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11) in brackets: Jesus writes on the ground, says 'Let the one without sin cast the first stone', and sends her away uncondemned, 'go and sin no more'. Then, still at Sukkot, Jesus says, 'I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness.' A long, increasingly heated debate follows about his testimony, his Father and his origin. To Jews who had believed in him, he says the truth will set them free; they protest that as Abraham's children they have never been slaves. The argument escalates to Jesus' charge that their desire to kill him shows the devil's parentage, not Abraham's. It climaxes in 'Before Abraham was, I am', and they pick up stones.
13228: The adultery story is missing from the earliest Greek manuscripts (such as P66, P75, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus), and in some later manuscripts it appears in other places, even in Luke. Most scholars, conservative and critical, think it was not part of John's original text, though many believe it preserves a genuine early tradition about Jesus. The rest of the chapter is the sharpest conflict in the Gospel, and its polemic has been abused more than almost any other text. Scholars widely believe its harshness reflects the bitter later conflict between John's community and synagogue leaders as well as the original setting.
13229:
During Sukkot, according to the Mishnah (Sukkah 5:2-4), four huge golden lamp-stands were lit in the Court of the Women in the temple. It was said that no courtyard in Jerusalem was not lit by their light, and devout men danced with torches through the night while Levites played music on the fifteen steps. Jesus speaks 'in the treasury' (John 8:20), which was in that same court. To say 'I am the light of the world' there was like pointing to the blazing lamps and saying, 'This is about me.'

Arguments about descent ('we are Abraham's children') were arguments about honour and identity. In ancient thought you resembled your father: actions revealed parentage.
13230:
The light recalls the pillar of fire that guided Israel in the wilderness (Exod 13:21), the very event Sukkot remembers, and Isaiah's servant as 'a light to the nations' (Isa 49:6). 'Before Abraham was, I am' echoes God's own name (Exod 3:14) and especially the 'I am he' of Isaiah (Isa 43:10-13), spoken by the one God who existed before all. The hearers understand it as a claim to divine identity, which is why they reach for stones as for blasphemy (Lev 24:16).

The 'children of the devil' language is family polemic. The Dead Sea Scrolls divide even Israel into 'sons of light' and 'sons of darkness'; the prophets called Israel's leaders 'rulers of Sodom' (Isa 1:10). Jesus is speaking to particular people seeking his death (John 8:40), using the logic that you show your father by your deeds, the same test 1 John 3:8-10 applies to Christians. It is not a statement about the Jewish people.
13231: John's community, in conflict with synagogue leaders, would hear their own arguments about Abraham, Moses and freedom. They would hear that Jesus is the light the Sukkot lamps celebrated. Later readers who were no longer a vulnerable minority would misuse the same words with terrible results.
13232: This chapter must be read with great care. It is a picture of Jesus revealing God's light and of truth that frees people from the slavery of sin, not a licence for contempt. The adultery story, whatever its textual history, shows Jesus protecting a vulnerable woman from a crowd and still calling her to a new life.
13233: The pillar of fire lighting Israel's way.
13235: God's name, 'I am who I am'.
13236: 'Before me no god was formed... I am he.'
13237: Abraham 'saw' the day of God's provision on Moriah, a Jewish background for John 8:56.
13238: John 8:44 shows that Jews are children of the devil — a reading used in medieval and modern antisemitism.
13239: Jesus addresses particular opponents seeking to kill him, using Jewish family polemic; the same test applies to anyone (1 John 3:8-10). It cannot rightly be applied to the Jewish people (Brown, Keener, Levine; Reinhartz warns of its real anti-Jewish effect).
13240: The man born blind and the fear of being put out
13241: Jesus' disciples ask whether a man born blind was punished for his own sin or his parents'. Jesus says neither: it is so God's works may be revealed. He spits on the ground, makes mud, anoints the man's eyes and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam ('Sent'). He comes back seeing. It is the Sabbath. The neighbours, the Pharisees and the man's parents are questioned; the parents answer cautiously because 'the Jews had already agreed that anyone who confessed Jesus to be Messiah would be put out of the synagogue' (John 9:22). The man grows bolder in each interview, from 'the man called Jesus' to 'a prophet' to worshipping Jesus as the Son of Man. He is thrown out. Jesus finds him and says he came so the blind might see and those who claim to see become blind.
13242:
John 9:22 is the first of three aposynagōgos ('put out of the synagogue') passages (also John 12:42 and John 16:2). In 1968 J. Louis Martyn proposed that John 9 should be read on two levels: the story of Jesus and the experience of John's community decades later, expelled from the synagogue. Martyn linked this to the Birkat ha-Minim, the 'blessing' (in fact a curse) against heretics in the Jewish daily prayer, said to have been revised at Yavneh around AD 85.

This theory has been widely debated. Reuven Kimelman (1981) and others showed there is no clear evidence that the first-century form targeted Christians, or that it was used empire-wide to expel them; the text mentioning Nazarenes (notzrim) comes from later manuscripts. Joel Marcus (2009) defends a modified version. Adele Reinhartz questions the expulsion theory itself. Most scholars today accept that some Jesus-followers experienced exclusion from local synagogues, but not a single, official decree.

The pool of Siloam from the Second Temple period was rediscovered in Jerusalem in 2004, a large stepped pool consistent with ritual washing.
13243: Many people assumed disability was punishment for sin, a view the book of Job had already challenged. Spittle was regarded in the ancient world as having healing power, and making mud could count as kneading, one of the activities forbidden on the Sabbath in later rabbinic lists. Synagogue membership meant much more than a weekly service: it was family, community, trade, burial and social belonging. Being 'put out' meant social death. The parents' fear is entirely understandable.
13244:
Opening the eyes of the blind was a sign of God's new age (Isa 35:5, Isa 42:7). Jesus as 'the light of the world' (John 9:5) continues the Sukkot theme, and Siloam was the pool from which the Sukkot water was drawn. Making clay and anointing may echo God forming Adam from the ground (Gen 2:7): a new creation for a man born blind.

The debate among the Pharisees is a genuine Jewish argument: some say 'This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath', but others ask, 'How can a sinner do such signs?' (John 9:16). The man reasons like a Torah student: 'God does not listen to sinners... if this man were not from God, he could do nothing' (John 9:31-33). The issue is the true reading of Moses.
13245: For a community that had paid the price of exclusion, the blind man would be a hero: someone whose witness grew under pressure, who lost his place in the synagogue but was found by Jesus. Fearful sympathisers would see themselves in the parents and be challenged.
13246: Disability is not punishment. Faith often grows step by step through questions. The chapter also warns any community — including churches — against excluding people whose experience does not fit its expectations, and asks who is really blind.
13247: The eyes of the blind opened in the coming age.
13249: God forms humanity from the dust of the ground.
13250: 'Who makes a person mute or deaf, seeing or blind? Is it not I, the Lord?'
13251: The gently flowing waters of Shiloah (Siloam).
13252: The Pharisees are hard-hearted legalists who simply hated Jesus.
13253: The Pharisees are divided (John 9:16) and argue from Torah; the story is about how people respond to new evidence. The 'put out of the synagogue' detail likely reflects later local conflict, though the Birkat ha-Minim link is debated (Martyn, Kimelman, Marcus, Reinhartz).
13254: The good shepherd and the feast of Dedication
13255: Jesus contrasts thieves and hired hands with the good shepherd who knows his sheep by name, leads them out, and lays down his life for them. 'I am the gate'; 'I am the good shepherd.' He has other sheep 'not of this fold' who will become one flock with one shepherd. Some say he is possessed; others ask whether a demon can open blind eyes. In winter, at the feast of Dedication (Hanukkah), Jesus walks in Solomon's Porch. Asked plainly if he is the Messiah, he says his works testify, his sheep hear his voice, no one will snatch them from his hand, and 'I and the Father are one'. When they move to stone him, he cites Psalm 82, 'I said, you are gods', and calls himself the one the Father consecrated and sent. He withdraws across the Jordan, where many believe.
13256: The shepherd discourse follows directly from chapter 9: the authorities who threw out the healed man are contrasted with the shepherd who finds him. Hanukkah celebrated the rededication of the temple in 164 BC by Judas Maccabeus after the Seleucid king Antiochus IV had defiled it (recorded in 1 Maccabees 4, a book outside the Protestant canon). It is the only mention of Hanukkah in the Bible.
13257: Shepherds in Judea often kept several flocks together overnight in a stone fold, with one gate. In the morning each shepherd called his own sheep, which recognised his voice. Some shepherds slept across the opening as a living gate. Hired hands were paid workers without the owner's stake in the flock. Hanukkah, in winter, featured lights and the reading of the story of the Maccabees, who resisted foreign tyranny and false shepherds. Solomon's Porch, a covered colonnade on the east side of the temple, was a natural place to walk in winter.
13258:
Ezekiel 34 is the key text: God condemns Israel's shepherds (its rulers) who fed themselves and not the flock, and promises, 'I myself will shepherd my sheep... I will set over them one shepherd, my servant David' (Ezek 34:11-24). Jesus claims both roles: God's own shepherding and the Davidic shepherd. Psalm 23 and Jeremiah 23:1-6 lie in the background.

At Hanukkah, the feast of the consecrated temple, Jesus says he is the one 'the Father consecrated' (hagiazō, John 10:36) — he is the dedicated temple. 'I and the Father are one' echoes the Shema, 'the Lord is one' (Deut 6:4): the sheep in his hand are in the Father's hand. His use of Psalm 82 is a rabbinic 'how much more' argument: if scripture can call those who received God's word 'gods', how much more the one God sent.
13259: A community that felt cast out would hear that the true shepherd knows them by name and that no one can snatch them away. Gentile believers would hear themselves as the 'other sheep', brought into the one flock of Israel's God, not a separate flock.
13260: The picture is deeply relational: being known by name and knowing a voice. Leaders are judged by whether they lay down their lives for the flock or use it. Security rests in God's hold, not in our grip.
13261: God himself shepherds and seeks the lost.
13264: 'I said, you are gods' — quoted by Jesus.
13265: The Shema: the Lord is one.
13266: The 'other sheep' are Gentiles who form a new, separate people that replaces Israel.
